title: Exact Expressive Power of Transformers with Padding
relevance_reason: Exact complexity-class characterization of looped (depth-recurrent) padded transformers as a function of loop count.
one_sentence: Proves that averaging-hard-attention transformers with polynomial padding recognize exactly FO-uniform TC0, and with O(log^d n) looping of a middle block recognize exactly FO-uniform TC^d, so polylog looping plus padding yields exactly FO-uniform NC.
key_contributions: Matching lower bound: poly-padded fixed-depth AHATs = FO-uniform TC0 (Theorem 1), resolving an open question from Pfau et al. 2024.

O(log^d n)-looped poly-padded AHATs = FO-uniform TC^d for d>=1 (Theorem 2); union over d = FO-uniform NC (Corollary 2.1), via a new TC^d-complete 'wide circuit evaluation' problem and transformer-implementable L reductions.
Uniformity collapse: FO-, L- and NL-uniform AC^d / TC^d coincide for d>=1 (Theorem 3); log and poly precision give identical power in these settings.

setup.model_sizes: Formal model: fixed parameters, fixed width, log or poly precision, masked pre-norm, causal masking, no positional encoding, averaging hard attention
setup.loops_test: Block B repeated d(n) = O(log^d n) times on inputs of length n
setup.baselines: Chain-of-thought transformers (prior theory, Merrill and Sabharwal 2023b)

claims.claim: Simulation (exact characterization, d=0): masked-pre-norm AHATs with polynomial padding recognize exactly FO-uniform TC0; n^k padding tokens give storage to resolve majority-logic formulas over k variables.
claims.evidence_quote: We show that averaging-hard-attention, masked-pre-norm transformers with polynomial padding recognize precisely the class FO-uniform TC0 of extremely parallelizable problems.

claims.claim: Simulation (exact characterization, looping): with O(log^d n) repetitions of a looped block and polynomial padding, transformers recognize exactly FO-uniform TC^d; looping adds depth with no extra parameters.
claims.evidence_quote: we prove that padded transformers with O(logd n) looping on inputs of length n recognize exactly the class FO-uniform TCd of moderately parallelizable problems.

claims.claim: Polylog looping + poly padding = FO-uniform NC, the parallel ceiling; consequently log/polylog-looped padded transformers solve problems believed outside TC0 (boolean formula evaluation, iterated matrix multiplication, graph connectivity, CFL recognition).
claims.evidence_quote: Thus log or polylog-looped transformers can solve many problems outside TC0 under standard complexity conjectures, including boolean formula evaluation, iterated matrix multiplication, graph connectivity, and context-free language recognition.

claims.claim: Positioning vs CoT: looping and padding are strictly weaker than CoT under standard conjectures (CoT reaches beyond NC) but preserve parallelism.
claims.evidence_quote: Thus, while looping and padding are not as powerful as CoT, our results suggest they are quite effective ways to expand transformers' expressive power while preserving parallelism.

claims.claim: Log-precision and poly-precision looped padded transformer classes are identical.
claims.evidence_quote: This shows that these two levels of precision lead to identical power for polylog-looped polynomially-padded transformers.

limitations: No experiments; learnability of looped layers is open; padding increases context length and memory; AHAT idealization (soft attention may not simulate hard attention at unbounded length); masked pre-norm assumption.
venue: 39th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2025).
builds_on: Merrill and Sabharwal 2025 (A little depth goes a long way)
survey_notes: Theory anchor for 'looping = depth scaling axis': exact class TC^d for log^d n loops, no new parameters. Loop count grows with input length (budget scales with n), a regime not used by any LM-scale looped model (fixed or small loop counts). Complements 2505.19245 (CoT vs loop separation) and 2605.30523 (which revisits which architectural choices matter for padded expressivity). Authors explicitly flag lack of empirical support.

title: Looped Transformers are Better at Learning Learning Algorithms
relevance_reason: Trains a single weight-tied GPT-2 layer looped with input injection to in-context learn function classes; foundational empirical paper for looped ICL theory.
one_sentence: A 1-layer GPT-2 block looped b times with input injection and a truncated loss over the last T loops in-context learns linear, sparse linear, decision-tree and 2-layer-NN functions, matching a 12-layer transformer with 1/12 of the parameters and converging to stable fixed points.
key_contributions: Training recipe for looped decoder transformers: input injection Y_{t+1}=M(Y_t+P), loss averaged over loop iterations b-T..b (truncated BPTT-like), with a schedule on b.

Looped 0.79M-parameter model matches the 9.48M 12-layer transformer on in-context regression families and beats it (and Lasso, at few samples) on sparse linear regression; learns with fewer distinct prompts.
Shows inductive bias toward simpler solutions, stable fixed points beyond trained loops (only with input injection), and that iso-depth (b=12) looping does not match the standard model.

setup.model_sizes: Looped: 1 layer, 0.79M params; standard: 12 layers, 9.48M params; GPT-2, D=256, 8 heads
setup.train_tokens_or_data: Synthetic in-context prompts following Garg et al. 2022 (d=20, k=40 for linear regression)
setup.loops_train: b in {12,20,30,40,50}, truncated window T in {5,10,15}; b=20,T=15 for linear regression; b=70 for decision trees; b=12 for 2-layer NN
setup.loops_test: Up to 100-200 loop iterations at inference
setup.baselines: 12-layer GPT-2 transformer (Garg et al.), least squares, Lasso, kNN, XGBoost, greedy tree learning
setup.benchmarks: In-context linear regression, sparse linear regression, decision trees, 2-layer ReLU nets, OpenML datasets (appendix)

claims.claim: A looped transformer matches a standard transformer on in-context data-fitting tasks with under 10% of its parameters.
claims.regime: iso_data; looped has 1/12 params and larger effective depth (b=20 vs 12 layers), so more inference FLOPs
claims.evidence_quote: Experimental results suggest that the looped transformer achieves performance comparable to the standard transformer in solving various data-fitting problems, while utilizing less than 10% of the parameter count.

claims.claim: At matched effective depth (b=12 loops of 1 layer vs 12 distinct layers), the looped model does not match the standard transformer; it needs more loops than layers (about 20 iterations of 1 layer to match 8 layers).
claims.evidence_quote: To match the performance of a standard transformer with L layers, the looped transformer needs more than L loop iterations, i.e. the effective depth of the looped transformer exceeds that of the standard transformer.

claims.claim: Input injection is necessary for stable extrapolation in loop count: without it, the weight-tied model diverges beyond the trained number of loops; with it, the model reaches a fixed point that persists past training iterations.
claims.evidence_quote: During inference, the weight-tying transformer will quickly diverge after the trained loop iterations.

claims.claim: Looped transformers show an inductive bias toward simpler (sparser) solutions: better on sparse linear regression and skewed covariance, worse under input-scale shift.
claims.evidence_quote: the looped transformer exhibits an inductive bias favoring simpler solutions when compared to the unlooped transformer.

claims.claim: The learned looped solver only emulates fixed-point iteration within the training distribution, with an error floor and limited OOD generalization; it does not recover a true algorithm.
claims.evidence_quote: As a result, our trained looped transformer fails to identify an actual algorithm that generalizes to any input distribution, but only emulates the algorithm with the particular input distribution it is trained on.

numbers.what: Parameter counts: standard 12-layer vs looped 1-layer
numbers.quote: In terms of the number of parameters, the unlooped transformer comprises 9.48M parameters, and the looped transformer uses 0.79M.

numbers.what: Sparse linear regression error at 40 in-context samples (Lasso / LS / looped / standard)
numbers.quote: with 40 in-context samples, the Lasso achieves a solution with an error of 1.32e-04, the Least Squares reaches 8.21e-14, the looped transformer achieves 6.12e-04, and the standard transformer achieves 0.0017.

numbers.what: Chosen loop hyperparameters for linear regression
numbers.quote: Guided by these criteria, we adopt b = 20 and T = 15 for the linear regression task.

numbers.what: Loop iterations of a 1-layer looped model needed to match an 8-layer transformer
numbers.quote: For instance, a looped transformer with a single layer requires roughly 20 iterations in order to achieve an 8-layer transformer's performance.

limitations: Solutions have an error floor and limited OOD generalization (scaled inputs); b and T require per-task tuning; larger T destabilizes training; only small synthetic ICL tasks.
venue: Published as a conference paper at ICLR 2024
survey_notes: Empirical anchor for the looped-ICL theory line (2410.21698, 2410.11268, 2410.08292 in theory_a, 2506.15329). The parameter-efficiency headline is not iso-FLOP: the looped model runs 20 loops vs 12 layers. At iso-effective-depth (b=12) it loses, consistent with the theory that looping trades parameters for more depth/iterations. Fixed-point behaviour beyond trained loops with input injection matches Bansal et al. 2022 (2202.05826) and contrasts with the divergence of plain weight-tying.

title: Universal interpolation for deep residual self-attention networks
relevance_reason: Depth-only expressivity with extreme parameter reuse (two frozen attention blocks reused across depth), motivated by looped transformers; block order and gains are task-dependent, so not a fixed loop.
one_sentence: Proves via geometric control theory that two frozen Gaussian-initialized single-head residual softmax attention blocks, applied in a task-dependent order with signs and durations, can map any batch of N n-token sequences to any other (universal interpolation), at continuous and finite depth; causal masking restricts this.
key_contributions: Formalizes exact vs universal interpolation and transfers Lie-rank criteria from continuous to finite-depth residual networks.

Noncausal attention: 2Nnd frozen Gaussian blocks suffice for universal interpolation (Theorem 3.3); with single-head width r>=d, only two blocks suffice for all N and n on a full-measure connected domain (Theorem 3.5).

Causal attention: first-token update is linear, so exact interpolation fails when batch size N exceeds token dimension d (Proposition 3.8); universality recovered within classes sharing first-token linear relations (Corollary 3.10).

setup.model_sizes: Token dimension d>=3, single-head attention of width r>=d (Theorem 3.5); no MLPs
setup.loops_test: Depth (number of block applications) depends on the interpolation problem; no explicit bound
setup.benchmarks: Numerical Lie-rank checks in PyTorch (Section M)

claims.claim: Universality (depth-only, two shared blocks): two frozen single-head residual softmax attention blocks with Gaussian projections achieve universal interpolation of sequence batches; only block order, signs and durations depend on the task.
claims.evidence_quote: Our main result establishes it for residual softmax attention using only two frozen single-head blocks with Gaussian-initialized projection matrices. The result holds at both continuous and finite depth.

claims.claim: With arbitrary heads, a dictionary of 2D (D = Nnd) Gaussian blocks gives universal interpolation on the full noncollinear domain, with block count growing with batch size.
claims.evidence_quote: to establish universal interpolation with frozen random noncausal attention blocks for any prescribed number of heads, using a number of blocks that grows linearly with the batch size (Theorem 3.3);

claims.claim: Negative result for causal attention: exact and universal interpolation on the full configuration space are impossible once batch size exceeds token dimension, because causal masking preserves linear relations among first tokens.
claims.evidence_quote: As a result, exact interpolation fails for N > d, whatever the number of heads (Proposition 3.8).

limitations: No depth bounds (depth may depend on endpoints); attention-only with no MLP; r<d case is conjectured from numerics only; trade-off between number of generators and required depth left open.
survey_notes: Gives the strongest 'depth alone suffices' statement: a fixed tiny parameter set with reuse is universal for interpolation, but with unbounded, task-dependent depth and schedule. Unlike circuit-complexity results (2505.18948), no resource bounds. Causal-masking obstruction is a distinct caveat relevant to decoder-only looped LMs. Not tested at LM scale.

title: On the Spatiotemporal Dynamics of Generalization in Neural Networks
relevance_reason: Weight-tied local convolutional rule iterated until a fixed point (neural cellular automaton) for length extrapolation; not a transformer and trained on single-step transitions.
one_sentence: Derives from locality, symmetry and stability postulates a neural cellular automaton (SEAD) trained on single-step transitions and iterated with argmax projection until a fixed point, reporting exact length extrapolation on parity, binary addition (16 to 10^6) and Rule 110.
key_contributions: Three postulates (finite-speed locality, spatiotemporal weight sharing, discrete-attractor stability) argued as necessary for length generalization.
SEAD: CNN kernel trained on one-step transitions, run at inference as a Relax-and-Project loop with argmax and fixed-point halting.
Exact extrapolation with tens of parameters; convergence steps adapt to input difficulty (O(L) for adversarial carries).

setup.model_sizes: 41-99 trainable parameters (task-dependent)
setup.train_tokens_or_data: Single-step transition supervision on sequences of length 16 (parity, addition) or 32 (Rule 110)
setup.loops_test: Iterate until fixed point; up to L+1 steps (10^6+1 for addition)
setup.benchmarks: Parity, binary addition (random and adversarial 1^L+1), Rule 110

claims.claim: A 99-parameter SEAD trained on length-16 addition achieves 100% exact match up to length 1,000,000, with convergence steps adapting to input difficulty.
claims.evidence_quote: Addition—achieving scale-invariant inference from L=16 to L=1,000,000 with 100% accuracy, exhibiting input-adaptive computation

claims.claim: Parity extrapolates from length 16 to 10^6 with inference steps exactly L+1, consistent with light-cone propagation at speed 1.
claims.evidence_quote: The model achieved perfect length generalization (from 16 to 106 , a generalization factor of 62,500x), and the inference steps 𝑇 were strictly equal to 𝐿 + 1

claims.claim: Supervision is on known single-step rules, not discovery from input-output data; this is the key caveat for comparison with end-to-end trained looped models.
claims.evidence_quote: It is important to emphasize that the model learns under supervised signals of known rules, not discovering rules from chaotic data—the latter is the harder “rule discovery” problem, left for future work.

numbers.what: Addition convergence steps, random vs adversarial, at L=10^4, 10^5, 10^6 (Table 3 rows)
Addition model size and training
numbers.quote: only 99 trainable parameters, trained for 5,000 steps on sequences of length 𝐿 = 16, with a total training time of about 24 seconds.

numbers.what: Parity model size
numbers.quote: The model has only 41 trainable parameters and converges in about 900 steps (~3 seconds) on a home computer (RTX 4080 Super).

limitations: Rules are learned with direct single-step supervision of known transitions; only simple tasks; no transformer or language experiments; the theory is postulate-based rather than proved; internally inconsistent parity parameter count (41 vs 57).
survey_notes: Extreme end of the 'iterate a local shared rule to a fixed point' design: convergence-based halting and discrete projection give exact extrapolation, but only with step-level supervision. Should not be compared with end-to-end looped transformer extrapolation results (2409.15647, 2202.05826) without that caveat. The paper reports the parity model as 41 parameters (Sec 4.1) and 57 parameters (Sec 4.2), an internal inconsistency.

title: Beyond the Training Horizon: Mechanisms and Limits of Length Generalization in Looped Transformers
relevance_reason: Mechanistic analysis of how two looped-transformer recipes extrapolate beyond the trained horizon and why they fail.
one_sentence: Mechanistically compares two looped-transformer recipes (Fan et al. 2025 MR-Loop with loops tied to input length; Kohli et al. 2026 DR-Loop with sampled loops) on composition tasks, finding distinct circuits, a shared 'computational status' code, error compounding at long horizons, and unfaithful shortcuts.
key_contributions: MR-Loop keeps a fixed accumulator at the [EQ] readout and advances relation selection one token per loop; DR-Loop propagates an advancing state frontier.
Both encode computational status (live vs consumed, fresh vs aged residual directions) that causally gates reuse, including beyond the training horizon.

Extreme-length failure from state degradation plus limited self-correction (survival/hazard account); extrapolation success need not imply faithful step-by-step trajectories, and depends on task compressibility.

setup.model_sizes: 3 shared transformer blocks, 2 heads, width 256, no positional embeddings
setup.train_tokens_or_data: Synthetic sequential composition tasks with final-answer supervision only
setup.loops_train: MR-Loop: K = input length n (trained up to n=12); DR-Loop: depth sampled independently of input length
setup.loops_test: MR-Loop K = n for longer n (20, 30); DR-Loop chosen at inference
setup.baselines: Two looped recipes compared; no non-looped baseline
setup.benchmarks: Polynomial iteration mod M, finite-state composition, knowledge-graph traversal

claims.claim: Under final-answer supervision, the two looped recipes learn mechanistically distinct recurrent algorithms (fixed readout accumulator vs advancing frontier).
claims.evidence_quote: MR-Loop updates an intermediate state at a fixed readout while advancing relation selection through adjacent-token interactions and a transferable progress cue. DR-Loop instead propagates intermediate states across relation positions, forming an advancing computational frontier.

claims.claim: Extrapolation has a finite range: MR-Loop final-answer accuracy with loops equal to input length drops to 70.3% at n=20 and 1.6% at n=30 (trained to n=12).
claims.evidence_quote: The observed extrapolation has a finite operating range: final-answer accuracy with R = n loops is 70.3% at n = 20 and 1.6% at n = 30, and the key-state cue weakens at larger hop indices.

claims.claim: Failure at extreme lengths comes from degradation of computation-supporting states plus limited self-correction, so errors compound geometrically in trajectory survival.
claims.evidence_quote: extreme-length generalization fails when repeated updates degrade the states needed for subsequent computation and the learned recurrence does not reliably repair them

claims.claim: Length generalization need not reflect faithful iterative computation; with compressible tasks models reach correct answers without exposing intermediate states.
claims.evidence_quote: Successful length generalization therefore demonstrates behavioral transfer to longer horizons, but does not, by itself, establish that the model executes the intended state-by-state procedure.

numbers.what: MR-Loop next-hop accuracy restored by transplanting [EQ] state from a length-20 prefix into a length-30 run (keys 12-19)
numbers.quote: raises mean native next-hop accuracy over keys 12 ≤ k ≤ 19 from 5.5% to 83.6% (Appendix G.1.1).

numbers.what: DR-Loop peak correct-entity probability on 29-hop inputs, hop 5 vs hop 16
numbers.quote: mean per-example peak correct-entity probability within the evaluation windows falls from 0.982 at hop 5 to 0.713 at hop 16 (Section G.2).

numbers.what: MR-Loop final-answer accuracy at n=20 and n=30 (trained n<=12)
numbers.quote: final-answer accuracy with R = n loops is 70.3% at n = 20 and 1.6% at n = 30

limitations: Not a controlled recurrence ablation (the two recipes differ in injection, normalization, masking, readout); tiny models on synthetic tasks; authors call for structure ablations and larger-scale tests.
builds_on: 2409.15647 (Fan et al. 2025, Looped Transformers for Length Generalization)
Labovich 2026 (Stability and generalization in looped transformers)
survey_notes: Key nuance for length-generalization claims of looped models: (i) extrapolation is bounded (MR-Loop collapses by 2.5x the training length on KG), (ii) failures are state-degradation plus no repair, consistent with stability analyses (2607.20594, 2410.23451), (iii) success can be via shortcuts, so 'learns the algorithm' claims require intermediate-state checks. Cross-ref 2604.07822 (DR-Loop source) and 2409.15647 (MR-Loop source).

title: Looped Transformers with Layer Normalization Provably Learn the Power Method
relevance_reason: Training-dynamics proof that a weight-tied (looped) linear transformer with normalization learns the power method, one iteration per loop.
one_sentence: Proves that a looped linear-attention transformer with RMS-style normalization, trained end-to-end by population gradient descent to predict a leading principal component, converges to the L-step power method (one iteration per loop), and that without normalization even layerwise-supervised training cannot match it.
key_contributions: Theorem 4.1: GD on an L-loop linear transformer with column normalization preserves a block structure and converges to the L-step power method, an 'algorithmic implicit bias' without step supervision.

Theorems 4.2/4.3/4.6: without LN a layer cannot exactly learn a power iteration and looping it gives a fixed suboptimal contraction factor; with LN the contraction approaches the optimal lambda_{r+1}/lambda_1.
OOD guarantee (Theorem 4.7): the learned looped model applies to any data matrix with unit-norm columns; small SGD experiments match the predicted Theta(t^{1/4}) weight growth.

setup.model_sizes: Linear (softmax removed) single-layer attention, merged key-query W and value V in R^{2d x 2d}; experiments d=16, n=32
setup.train_tokens_or_data: Population GD in theory; experiments 10000 training matrices, 2000 epochs, SGD lr 0.1
setup.loops_test: L, and looping the one-layer module at inference for OOD analysis
setup.benchmarks: Principal component prediction on rotation-invariant unit-column data

claims.claim: Optimization/learnability: gradient descent on a looped linear transformer with LN, supervised only on the principal-component target, converges to the power method with one power iteration per loop.
claims.evidence_quote: We prove that a looped linear transformer with LN, trained by gradient descent, converges to a solution that implements the power method, with each self-attention layer performing one power iteration.

claims.claim: Separation in training outcome: even with layerwise power-iteration supervision, a transformer without LN cannot exactly learn the power method, whereas with LN it can, giving a provable performance gap.
claims.evidence_quote: even with layerwise guidance from power iterations, a transformer without LN cannot exactly learn the power method, whereas the corresponding transformer with LN can, leading to a provable performance gap in principal component prediction.

claims.claim: Looping the LN-trained module yields exponential error decay whose contraction factor approaches the optimal power-method rate; without LN the factor is fixed and suboptimal.
claims.evidence_quote: In contrast, for a transformer without LN, irrespective of the training target in (4.4), looping the learned module also results in exponential error decay, but with a fixed and suboptimal factor

numbers.what: Predicted growth rate of active weights under GD
numbers.quote: The active parameters also display a polynomial growth trend, and the log-log plots are consistent with the Θ(t1/4 ) scaling predicted by Theorem 4.1.

numbers.what: Experimental configuration
numbers.quote: We set d = 16, n = 32, and L = 10, and plot the heatmaps of the matrices V and W after 2000 training iterations together with the evolution of the learned weights.

limitations: Linear attention (softmax removed), specific initialization, population gradient, rotation-invariant unit-column data; experiments are small illustrations.
builds_on: 2410.08292 (Gatmiry et al. 2024, looped linear transformers learn multi-step GD)
survey_notes: Supports the claim that normalization between loops matters for learned looped dynamics (relevant to normalization design choices in LM-scale looped models; cross-check with lineage_architecture records). A learnability result (what GD finds), complementing constructive results (2402.01107, 2301.13196). Weights diverge during training, so the LN is what keeps outputs bounded. Not tested at LM scale.

title: Thinking Deeper, Not Longer: Memory-Efficient Test-Time Reasoning with Depth-Recurrent Transformers for Compositional Generalization
relevance_reason: Weight-tied depth-recurrent transformer core with gated recurrence; controlled extrapolation, supervision and halting ablations.
one_sentence: A sub-1M-parameter shared-weight transformer block, stabilized by final-step-only ('silent thinking') loss, LayerScale and an identity-biased gate, extrapolates in depth on graph reachability, nested Boolean logic and relational text; per-step supervision and ACT halting hurt extrapolation.
key_contributions: Stability recipe for 20+ recurrence steps: final-output-only supervision, LayerScale init 1e-4, gated recurrence with gate bias -2.0 (identity-biased).

Computational frontier: accuracy rises once thinking steps meet task depth; recurrence extrapolates on graph reachability where fixed-depth models collapse and matches fixed-depth transformers with 4-6.4x parameters on sequence tasks.

Negative results: intermediate per-step supervision induces shortcuts and kills 10-hop extrapolation; ACT halting saturates near 4 ponder steps and fails OOD; memory stays flat vs CoT KV-cache growth.

setup.model_sizes: Recurrent core 0.2M (graph) to 1.0M (sequence tasks); fixed-depth baselines 0.5M-6.4M
setup.train_tokens_or_data: Synthetic graph reachability (1-5 hops), nested Boolean expressions, CLUTRR-inspired family relational text (depths 2-5)
setup.loops_train: Step ranges [5,8] graph, [4,16] nested expr., [1,12] family
setup.loops_test: Up to 20 (graph), 24 (nested expr.), 20 (family)
setup.baselines: Fixed-depth transformer, fixed-depth GNN, Universal Transformer with ACT, ablation without LayerScale and gate
setup.benchmarks: Graph reachability, nested Boolean logic, relational composition over text; ID and OOD (deeper) accuracy

claims.claim: Depth recurrence extrapolates beyond training depth on graph reachability where fixed-depth models barely extrapolate, and on sequence tasks comes within two points of fixed-depth transformers with 4-6.4x more parameters.
claims.regime: iso_data; parameters not matched (recurrent has fewer), compute not matched
claims.evidence_quote: Depth recurrence extrapolates beyond the training range: it succeeds on the graph task where fixed-depth models barely extrapolate, and on the two sequence tasks comes within two points of fixed-depth Transformers that use 4–6.4× more parameters.

claims.claim: Intermediate per-step supervision harms depth extrapolation: even alpha=0.1 per-step loss drops 10-hop accuracy to chance, while final-step-only training reaches 84%.
claims.evidence_quote: On the graph task, whose adjacency mask makes propagation depth verifiable, intermediate per-step supervision—a standard recipe for deep iterative models—consistently harms this extrapolation.

claims.claim: Learned ACT halting does not extrapolate: the Universal Transformer's ponder budget saturates near 4 steps where 8-12 are needed, returning to chance OOD on graph reachability.
claims.evidence_quote: because its learned halting saturates at ≈4 ponder steps where 8–12 are structurally required and the ponder penalty rewards early stopping.

claims.claim: The stability recipe mainly reduces seed variance rather than raising mean accuracy (graph OOD 62-76 across seeds without it).
claims.evidence_quote: ablating our stability recipe (last row: no LayerScale, no gate) leaves ID and mean OOD accuracy essentially unchanged but collapses training stability: the ablated model's graph OOD swings from 62 to 76 across seeds where ours varies by 0.2.

limitations: Sub-1M models; hand-designed perception interfaces per task; externally fixed step count (no working halting); integration with pretrained LLMs untested.
survey_notes: Probably the same work as theory_a's untitled-id entry 'Thinking Deeper, Not Longer: Depth-Recurrent Transformers for Compositional Generalization' (earlier title); deduplicate. Contradiction to flag: per-step (deep) supervision hurts depth extrapolation here, while deep supervision is central to recursive-reasoning models (HRM/TRM lineage) and Bansal et al.'s progressive loss helps extrapolation (2202.05826, 2405.17399). The difference: progressive loss trains final output from random truncated starts, not intermediate readouts. ACT halting failure OOD agrees with learned-halting critiques. Comparisons are not iso-param or iso-FLOP: fixed-depth baselines are larger.

title: Loop, Think, & Generalize: Implicit Reasoning in Recurrent-Depth Transformers
relevance_reason: Controlled from-scratch study of looped transformers for systematic generalization and depth extrapolation in implicit multi-hop reasoning, with iso-effective-depth baselines.
one_sentence: 4-layer GPT-2 blocks looped R times on synthetic knowledge-graph multi-hop queries achieve systematic generalization via three-stage grokking and extrapolate to deeper hops by scaling inference loops, unlike vanilla transformers of matched effective depth, but suffer overthinking.
key_contributions: Systematic generalization on 2-hop composition of unseen facts emerges for R>=2 loops through a memorization -> ID -> OOD grokking sequence; an iso-FLOP 8-layer vanilla model never generalizes OOD.
Depth extrapolation unlocked by more inference loops; training-loop budget sets the extrapolation range, Poisson-sampled dynamic recurrence increases learnable recursion depth.
Overthinking: logit margin peaks then declines with extra loops; input injection does not fix it; KL+entropy adaptive halting saves compute.

setup.model_sizes: GPT-2-style recurrent block of 4 layers, embedding dimension 768, 12 heads; vanilla baselines 4, 8, 16, 24 layers
setup.train_tokens_or_data: Synthetic KGs: 2000 entities/200 relations (systematicity, 40k atomic + 273.6k inferred facts); 200 entities/10 relations with up to 40-hop facts and curriculum (extrapolation)
setup.loops_train: Fixed R in {1,...,8} or dynamic R ~ clip(Poisson(lambda), 2, 8)
setup.loops_test: Up to about 25+ iterations; adaptive halting via KL and entropy thresholds
setup.baselines: Vanilla transformers (R=1 with 4 layers; 8/16/24 layers at matched effective depth)
setup.benchmarks: Synthetic 2-hop systematic generalization and k-hop depth extrapolation

claims.claim: Looped models (R>=2) achieve systematic generalization on unseen fact compositions while a vanilla 4-layer model (R=1, same params) and an iso-FLOP 8-layer vanilla model at matched effective depth fail.
claims.regime: iso_param (vs R=1); iso_effective_depth and iso_infer_flop (vs 8-layer vanilla)
claims.evidence_quote: We compare against an iso-FLOP 8-layer vanilla transformer with matched effective depth. The vanilla model exhibits only two training stages and fails to achieve non-zero systematic generalization regardless of training time

claims.claim: Scaling inference-time recurrence enables extrapolation to deeper compositions; the max training iterations determine the extrapolation range (R=6 reaches 14-hop, R=8 reaches 19-hop when trained up to 12-hop).
claims.evidence_quote: increasing the number of training-time iterations substantially improves extrapolation when scaling inference-time iterations (e.g. R = 6 extrapolates up to 14-hop, while R = 8 reaches 19-hop).

claims.claim: Deeper vanilla transformers (8/16/24 layers) improve ID generalization but remain weaker than looped models of the same effective depth and show no OOD depth extrapolation.
claims.evidence_quote: However, their ID generalization remains weaker than recurrent-depth models with the same effective depth. More importantly, the vanilla models still do not exhibit OOD generalization to more complex samples

claims.evidence_quote: Note that although previous work mitigates overthinking by injecting inputs information in every iteration (Bansal et al., 2022; Geiping et al., 2025), we find that such methods do not resolve the issue in implicit reasoning.

Contradiction: input injection is reported not to fix overthinking here, whereas Bansal et al. (2202.05826) and Geiping et al. use it against overthinking. title: Revisiting Padded Transformer Expressivity: Which Architectural Choices Matter and Which Don't
relevance_reason: Exact characterizations of looped padded transformers across precision, width, attention type and uniformity.
one_sentence: Shows that polynomially padded transformers are robust to attention type (softmax vs average-hard), width and uniformity, with precision and depth deciding expressivity: constant precision gives AC^0 and growing precision TC^0, and log^d N looping gives FO-uniform AC^d resp. TC^d.
key_contributions: Padded L-uniform constant-precision transformers = L-uniform AC0; growing-precision ones = L-uniform TC0, regardless of width, for both SMATs and AHATs (given volume Omega(log N)).
Looping: Theta(log^d N)-looped constant-precision padded transformers = FO-uniform AC^d; growing-precision = FO-uniform TC^d (Theorem 5.1); both approach NC.
No gain from width or precision beyond logarithmic; suggests spending sequential budget on looping rather than precision.

setup.model_sizes: Formal: width D(N), precision b(N), volume b*D >= Omega(log N); SMAT and AHAT
setup.loops_test: Theta(log^d N) loops for input length N

claims.claim: Simulation (looping): log^d N-looped padded transformers reach FO-uniform AC^d with constant precision and FO-uniform TC^d with growing precision.
claims.evidence_quote: Furthermore, looping enables sequential processing analogous to circuits: logd N -looped constantprecision transformers reach FO-uniform ACd , and growing-precision ones reach FO-uniform TCd .

claims.claim: Robustness: once precision is logarithmic, attention type, width and further precision do not change padded expressivity; precision and depth are the main factors.
claims.evidence_quote: Interestingly, growing width or precision beyond logarithmic does not increase expressivity, and all our results hold for both softmax and average hard attention transformers.

claims.claim: Resource-allocation implication: given a sequential budget, spend only log N on precision and the rest on looping, since expressivity scales with looping but not with extra precision (expressivity only, not learnability).
claims.evidence_quote: Given a budget of, e.g., logd N sequential steps, our results suggest devoting only log N of those to numeric precision and the remaining logd−1 N ones to looping

limitations: Expressivity only (no learnability claims); insufficient-volume (o(log N)) regime remains uncharacterized; looping count grows with input length.
venue: Proceedings of the 43 rd International Conference on Machine Learning, Seoul, South Korea. PMLR 306, 2026.
survey_notes: Extends 2505.18948 to constant precision (AC^d instead of TC^d) and softmax attention; addresses the AHAT idealization criticism of 2505.18948. The constant-precision result (AC^d) is the regime closest to low-precision deployed LMs; contrast with fixed-precision expressivity of looped padded transformers (title-only entry in this group, not read).

title: Recurrent neural networks approximate continuous functions
relevance_reason: Universality for a fixed-weight ReLU map iterated on its own state (input only at t=0), i.e. a looped network where accuracy is bought with more iterations; not a transformer.
one_sentence: Proves that every continuous function on [-1,1] is uniformly approximated by iterating a single fixed ReLU RNN of hidden size at most 5320, with accuracy improving only through longer runtime; polynomials get exponential rates, and runtime is shown to be an unavoidable resource.
key_contributions: Fixed-network approximation paradigm: for all f exists one RNN such that for all eps, running long enough gives error < eps (Theorem 3.1), with f-independent hidden size <= 5320 and weights <= 5(1+||f||_inf).
Exponential error decay 2*2^{-t/t_a} for polynomials (Theorem 3.2), optimal for x^2 by a breakpoint-count lower bound; rates for general f tied to Chebyshev-series convergence.
Proof tool: Turing machine with neural units (TMNU) simulated by RNNs with explicit size and weight bounds.

setup.model_sizes: ReLU RNN, hidden state dimension <= 5320
setup.loops_test: Runtime t -> infinity; input fed only at t=0

claims.claim: Universality via iteration: each continuous function on [-1,1] is uniformly approximated by the time evolution of a single fixed-weight, fixed-width ReLU RNN; accuracy increases only with runtime.
claims.evidence_quote: More precisely, each such function is uniformly approximated by the time evolution of a single ReLU recurrent neural network with fixed weights and fixed hidden dimension.

claims.claim: Resource bound: hidden dimension at most 5320 independent of f; weights bounded by 5(1 + sup norm of f).
claims.evidence_quote: Surprisingly perhaps, and in sharp contrast to the main result of [14], the hidden state dimension of the RNN R does not depend on the function f .

claims.claim: Lower bound: runtime is unavoidable; a fixed-size network run for fixed time is a depth-(t0+1) ReLU net whose breakpoints limit accuracy, so error for x^2 cannot decay faster than exponentially in t.
claims.evidence_quote: We complement the construction with minimax lower bounds showing that runtime is not merely a proof artifact, but an unavoidable resource in this fixed-network approximation paradigm.

numbers.what: Hidden state dimension bound for the universal approximating RNN
numbers.quote:
Moreover, the hidden state dimension and the magnitude of the weights of R satisfy

m(R) ≤ 5320, and M(R) ≤ 5 1 + ∥f ∥L∞ ([−1,1]) .

limitations: One-dimensional inputs on [-1,1]; constructive, not learned; large constants; real-valued (not fixed-precision) weights.
builds_on: Hutter et al. (RNN approximation paradigm, ref [14])
survey_notes: Formal statement of 'accuracy from more loops, not more parameters' for a looped ReLU map: the purest theoretical analog of test-time depth scaling. Contrasts with 2605.10878, which needs fixed precision for its complexity link; here real weights are used. Not tested empirically.

title: Beyond Memorization: Extending Reasoning Depth with Recurrence, Memory and Test-Time Compute Scaling
relevance_reason: Compares depth extension via ACT layer repetition (in-depth looping), segment-level memory recurrence, RL and CoT on a controlled multi-step benchmark; looping is one of several arms.
one_sentence: On a 1D cellular-automaton benchmark with disjoint train/test rules, 4-layer models solve one-step prediction but collapse at k>=2 look-ahead; ACT-based layer repetition adds about one effective step, GRPO reaches k=3, and token-level CoT reaches k=4.
key_contributions: 1dCA-Reasoning benchmark separating rule induction from multi-step state propagation, with held-out rules to exclude memorization.
Depth, not width, drives multi-step accuracy: 1-2 step accuracy saturates after 4-6 layers, 3-step improves to ~12 layers, 4-step stays poor up to 16 layers.
Depth extension: ACT (layer-wise or whole-model repetition) adds ~+1 effective step at fixed parameters; fixed-computation-time controls are mixed; explicit CoT supervision is the only route to k=4.

setup.model_sizes: 4-layer GPT-NeoX with d_model=128 and 4 heads (baseline); depth sweeps to 16 layers; LSTM, Mamba, ARMT
setup.train_tokens_or_data: 1dCA orbits (W=20 cells, radius 2), disjoint train/test rule sets; group multiplication (appendix)
setup.loops_train: ACT halting per layer (LACT) or whole model (MACT); fixed-computation-time control uses 3 iterations
setup.loops_test: ACT-determined
setup.baselines: Fixed-depth transformers of 4-16 layers, LSTM, Mamba, ARMT, SFT, GRPO, CoT
setup.benchmarks: 1dCA Orbit-State and Orbit-Orbit look-ahead k in {1,2,3,4}; Handsup natural-language proxy for LLMs; group multiplication

claims.claim: Fixed-depth 4-layer models solve next-step prediction but collapse for look-ahead k>=2 (0.95 at k=1, 0.40 at k=2, below 0.25 for k=3,4).
claims.evidence_quote: While the average accuracy for next-state prediction (O-S task with k = 1) was 0.95, it dropped to 0.40 for k = 2 and fell below 0.25 for k = 3 and k = 4.

claims.claim: ACT-style adaptive repetition adds about one effective reasoning step to transformer-based models without new parameters, with diminishing returns past k=3.
claims.evidence_quote: Adding Adaptive Computation Time (ACT) to a Transformer consistently shifts the depth frontier without increasing parameters, with diminishing returns past k≈3.

claims.claim: Extending effective depth via recurrence, memory or test-time compute helps but remains bounded; explicit CoT supervision achieves >90% up to k=4.
claims.evidence_quote: With stepwise targets, GPT-NeoX attains > 90% accuracy for k≤4 (Figure 4(c)), showing that explicit supervision can elicit deeper computation given the availability of intermediate labels.

claims.claim: Adaptive vs fixed loop count is inconclusive: a fixed 3-step control improved some settings and hurt others.
claims.evidence_quote: In O-S setting, FCT improved the exact match in look-ahead 2, 3 for GPTNeox, but performed worse in look-ahead 2 for ARMT. In contrast, in the O-O setting, FCT showed reduced performance for both GPTNeox and ARMT in look-ahead 2, 3, 4.

numbers.what: 4-layer GPT-NeoX exact match at look-ahead k=1 / k=2
numbers.quote: While the average accuracy for next-state prediction (O-S task with k = 1) was 0.95, it dropped to 0.40 for k = 2

numbers.what: Depth sweep result
numbers.value: 1-2 step saturates after 4-6 layers; 3-step improves to ~12 layers
numbers.quote: Figure 3 (a) shows that accuracy for one- and two-step prediction saturates after 4–6 layers. Three-step prediction, however, continues to improve up to about 12 layers

limitations: Small models; ACT budget small (upper bound about 3 steps); only cellular automata and group multiplication; LLM evaluation via natural-language proxy with imperfect answer extraction.
survey_notes: Evidence that small-budget learned halting gives only modest depth gains on rule-chaining tasks, consistent with 2603.21676's finding that ACT halting saturates and fails OOD. Explicit CoT outperforms latent depth extension when step labels exist, which bears on the loop vs CoT comparison (contrast theoretical claims in 2505.19245 that loops are more efficient for parallelizable tasks: 1dCA rollout is sequential in k).

title: To CoT or To Loop? A Formal Comparison Between Chain-of-Thought and Looped Transformers
relevance_reason: Formal two-way separation between looped transformers and chain of thought; superseded by 2509.25239 per its own header.
one_sentence: Shows looped transformers evaluate computation DAGs in loops proportional to graph depth while CoT needs steps proportional to graph size, giving strict separations favoring loops at polylog steps; conversely probabilistic CoT can approximately count self-reducible problems where deterministic loops cannot (if FPTAS != FPRAS).
key_contributions: DAG simulation: CoT simulates any bounded-fan-in poly-size DAG in steps proportional to its size (Theorem 4.4); looped TF in loops proportional to its depth, under linear parallel space and output-bound assumptions (Theorem 4.7).

Circuit equivalence: LOOP[T(n), poly, log n] = poly-size threshold circuits of depth T(n) (Theorem 4.11); separations CoT[log^k n] strictly within LOOP[log^k n] if TC^{k-1} != NC^k or TC^{k-1} != TC^k (Theorems 4.12-4.13); LIN, MATCH, FCFL in LOOP[log^2 n] but not CoT[log^2 n].

Reverse separation: assuming FPTAS != FPRAS, probabilistic CoT approximately counts some self-reducible relation in poly time while no deterministic looped TF can with poly loops (Theorem 5.6); weak CoT + self-consistency suffices.

setup.model_sizes: Nonuniform, poly(n) embedding size, log or constant precision, saturated attention, optional MoE FFN
setup.loops_test: T(n) loops with loop-dependent positional encodings; polylogarithmic regime for separations
setup.baselines: Chain of thought with T(n) decoding steps

claims.claim: Simulation: looped TF computes a DAG in loops proportional to its depth (parallel, layer-wise), whereas CoT requires steps proportional to its size (sequential topological order).
claims.evidence_quote: Theorem 4.4 shows that CoT simulates computations by decoding nodes in topological order, whereas Theorem 4.7 shows that Looped TF simulates computations in a layer-wise and parallel fashion.

claims.claim: Separation (loops > CoT): at the same polylogarithmic budget, CoT[log^k n] is strictly contained in LOOP[log^k n] under standard circuit conjectures; e.g., linear equations, bipartite perfect matching and fixed-CFL membership are in log^2 n loops but not log^2 n CoT steps.
claims.evidence_quote: These results show that, under the same polylogarithmic number of steps or loops, Looped TF can simulate parallel computations more efficiently than CoT.

claims.claim: Separation (CoT > loops): with stochastic decoding, CoT can approximately count solutions of some self-reducible relation, which no deterministic looped TF can do with polynomially many loops, assuming FPTAS != FPRAS.
claims.evidence_quote: Assuming that FPTAS = ̸ FPRAS, there exists a relation R such that a probabilistic CoT can approximate the count |R(x)| within any desired relative error ε > 0 with high probability in polynomial time

claims.claim: Looped TF with T(n) loops (poly width, log precision) is equivalent to nonuniform threshold circuits of polynomial size and depth T(n).
claims.evidence_quote: a decision problem L belongs to the class LOOP[T (n), poly(n), log n] if and only if L is decidable by nonuniform families of threshold circuits of polynomial size and depth T (n).

limitations: Nonuniform, poly-width constructions; looped simulation needs linear parallel space and bounded outputs; no experiments; superseded by 2509.25239.
survey_notes: Superseded: the paper states it is outdated and points to 2509.25239 (in theory_a); cite the newer version for final statements. Core of 'looped vs CoT': loops win on parallelizable (shallow-wide DAG) problems at equal step budgets, CoT wins on randomized approximate inference. Consistent with 2505.18948 (loops+padding = NC, CoT reaches beyond). The empirical counterpoint 2508.16745 (CoT beats ACT-style depth extension on sequential CA rollouts) is consistent with the theory since that task is sequential.

title: Neural Algorithmic Reasoning for Hypergraphs with Looped Transformers
relevance_reason: Constructive simulation of hypergraph algorithms by constant-size looped transformers.
one_sentence: Extends looped-transformer graph-algorithm simulation (2402.01107) to hypergraphs: constant-width, 10-11-layer looped transformers with 3 heads simulate a hypergraph-to-graph degradation (enabling Dijkstra, BFS, DFS) and Helly's algorithm, for sizes bounded by numerical precision.
key_contributions: Degradation mechanism: a 10-layer, 3-head, O(1)-width looped transformer implicitly converts incidence to adjacency so graph algorithms run on hypergraphs (Theorem 4.1).
Hyperedge-aware encoding: an 11-layer, 3-head, O(1)-width looped transformer simulates Helly's algorithm (Theorem 4.2).
Graph size bounded by O(1/delta_hat) where delta_hat is the representable minimum increment angle (precision-limited); extensions to hypergraph motif algorithms.

setup.model_sizes: 10 layers (degradation) or 11 layers (Helly), 3 heads per layer, O(1) feature dimension
setup.loops_test: Iterations of the simulated algorithm (until termination)

claims.claim: Simulation: a constant-size looped transformer (10 layers, 3 heads, O(1) width) simulates hypergraph degradation for up to O(1/delta_hat) vertices and hyperedges, enabling graph algorithms such as Dijkstra on hypergraphs.
claims.evidence_quote: consisting of 10 layers, where each layer includes 3 attention heads with feature dimension of O(1). This transformer can simulate the degradation operation (Algorithm 2) for hypergraphs

claims.claim: Simulation: an 11-layer, 3-head, constant-width looped transformer simulates Helly's algorithm on weighted hypergraphs, with size limited by precision.
claims.evidence_quote: consisting of 11 layers, where each layer includes 3 attention heads with feature dimension of O(1). This transformer can simulate the Helly algorithm (Algorithm 5) for weighted hypergraphs

limitations: Constructive existence only; no learning or experiments; problem size bounded by numerical precision.
survey_notes: Incremental extension of 2402.01107 to hypergraphs; same constant-width, precision-limited simulation paradigm. Purely constructive; untested.

title: On the Role of Depth and Looping for In-Context Learning with Task Diversity
relevance_reason: Depth lower/upper bounds for task-diverse in-context linear regression and a provable robustness advantage of looped (weight-shared) over multilayer transformers.
one_sentence: For in-context linear regression with covariance condition numbers in [1, kappa], proves log(kappa) (unrestricted) and sqrt(kappa) (restricted) depth lower bounds with matching constructions, shows multilayer global minimizers can fail under exponentially small distribution shift, and that looped transformers match the expressivity while being provably robust and depth-monotone.
key_contributions: Depth lower bounds Omega(log kappa) (unrestricted attention) and Omega(sqrt kappa) (restricted) for task-diverse ICL linear regression (Theorem 1); matching Chebyshev-iteration construction (Theorem 2) and residual-norm adaptive termination (Theorem 3).

Robustness separation: some multilayer global minimizers incur constant OOD loss under Wasserstein shift O(L d^{-1} 9^{-L}) (Theorem 6), while looped global minimizers extrapolate to distributions on the same support when training is right-spread-out (Theorem 7).

Monotonicity: if loss decreases monotonically with depth for every covariance, the layers must be equal (looped) (Theorem 8); experiments (d=10, n=20) confirm looped models are competitive in depth and more robust OOD.

setup.model_sizes: Linear (restricted) attention, 1 layer looped L times vs L distinct layers; d=10, n=20 in experiments
setup.train_tokens_or_data: Synthetic in-context linear regression with covariance s*I, s from Unif([1,kappa]) or a mixture of k covariances in [1,8]
setup.loops_train: L loops (matched to L layers of the multilayer baseline)
setup.loops_test: L; adaptive termination via residual norm (theory)
setup.baselines: Multilayer linear transformer with L distinct layers
setup.benchmarks: Test loss in- and out-of-distribution (window w around train covariances, up to 0.5)

claims.claim: Lower bound: solving task-diverse in-context linear regression requires Omega(log kappa) linear-attention layers (or Omega(sqrt kappa) under restricted attention), and multilayer transformers match these bounds.
claims.evidence_quote: we show theoretical lower bounds of log(κ) (or κ) linear attention layers in the unrestricted (or restricted) attention setting and, (b) we show that multilayer Transformers can indeed solve such tasks with a number of layers that matches the lower bounds.

claims.claim: Separation in robustness: multilayer transformers are not robust to distribution shifts as small as O(e^{-L}) in Wasserstein distance, whereas looped transformers have similar expressivity and are provably robust under mild assumptions.
claims.evidence_quote: multilayer Transformers are not robust to even distributional shifts as small as O(e−L ) in Wasserstein distance, where L is the depth of the network. We then demonstrate that Looped Transformers

claims.claim: Looped models are the only multilayer transformers with loss monotone in depth across all covariance distributions, making them natural for early exit.
claims.evidence_quote: if a multilayer model has monotonically decreasing error with depth for a diverse set of distributions, then it must be a looped model. This suggests that looped models are naturally suited for early-exiting strategies.

claims.claim: Empirically, L loops of one layer are competitive with L distinct layers in-distribution and more robust out-of-distribution.
claims.evidence_quote: We see that in all settings the looped model is more robust than the multilayer model, especially on the left plot where there is least diversity in the training distribution, as predicted by the theory.

numbers.what: Experimental dimensions
numbers.quote: we work with d = 10 dimensional inputs and each input instance consists of n = 20 pairs of (x, y) in the context.

limitations: Linear attention, realizable linear regression, isotropic-scaled covariances in experiments; robustness theorem needs right-spread-out training distributions.
survey_notes: Gives a theoretical reason for the OOD robustness of looped ICL observed empirically in 2311.12424: weight tying constrains the global minimizer to a single iterative update that extrapolates, while untied layers can overfit to training covariances. Also supports looped models for early exit (monotone loss). Uses iso-effective-depth comparisons (L loops vs L layers), so looped models have 1/L the parameters.

title: ALTA: Compiler-Based Analysis of Transformers
relevance_reason: Compiler from programs with loops to weight-shared / Universal Transformers; constructive length-invariant algorithms plus learnability analysis of looped models.
one_sentence: Introduces ALTA, a RASP-like language with loops that compiles to weight-shared/Universal Transformer encoders, constructing length-invariant parity and addition and a 100% SCAN solver, and shows end-to-end training fails to find these sequential algorithms even when expressible, preferring fewest-layer solutions.
key_contributions: ALTA language, interpreter and compiler to Transformers with layer-wise weight sharing and dynamic halting (Universal Transformers), with sparse MLP transition rules.

Constructive results: a weight-shared encoder with relative positions computes parity for any length with finite parameters; addition of unbounded integers in N+2 layers; SUBLEQ interpreter; SCAN shift-reduce parser at 100% accuracy (up to 512 layers).

Learnability tools: trace supervision and program minimality w.r.t. a training set; end-to-end trained models mimic the shallow Sum+Modulo parity program and deeper models (to 256+256 layers) do not improve SCAN generalization.

setup.model_sizes: Compiled models; SCAN model needs fewer than 2,000 MLP hidden dimensions; trained variants up to 256 encoder + 256 decoder layers
setup.train_tokens_or_data: Parity (train length <= 20, test 21-40), addition, SCAN splits
setup.loops_train: Layers = loop iterations of compiled program; dynamic halting for addition
setup.loops_test: N+2 layers for N-digit addition; up to 512 layers for SCAN
setup.baselines: End-to-end trained transformers with and without weight sharing; trace-supervised models
setup.benchmarks: Parity, multi-digit addition, SUBLEQ, SCAN (length and MCD splits)

claims.claim: Simulation: weight-shared / Universal Transformer encoders can express length-invariant algorithms for parity and addition and solve SCAN without scratchpad decoding.
claims.evidence_quote: ALTA allows us to constructively show how Transformers can represent length-invariant algorithms for computing parity and addition, as well as a solution to the SCAN benchmark of compositional generalization tasks, without requiring intermediate scratchpad decoding steps.

claims.claim: Resource bound: the compiled addition program needs N+2 layers (loop iterations) for N-digit inputs, and its minimal version trained on <=3-digit data generalizes to unbounded lengths.
claims.evidence_quote: The number of layers required to compute the sum is N + 2, where N is the number of digits in the larger of the two inputs.

claims.claim: Learnability gap: end-to-end trained weight-shared transformers behave like the shallow Sum+Modulo parity program (no generalization to more ones than seen), not the length-invariant sequential program, despite it being expressible.
claims.evidence_quote: However, in practice, all variants exhibit behavior similar to that of the minimal Sum + Modulo program, i.e., they exhibit some degree of length generalization but do not generalize to examples with more ones than were seen during training.

claims.claim: More layers do not help end-to-end SCAN generalization even up to 256 encoder and 256 decoder layers.
claims.evidence_quote: However, all generalize poorly on the test splits, and increasing the number of layers does not improve generalization.

numbers.what: Rule counts of minimal parity programs (Sequential Relative vs Sum+Modulo)
numbers.quote: While the minimal Sequential (Relative) program contains 7 rules and the minimal Sum + Modulo program contains 31 rules, our results show that end-to-end model behavior is more consistent with the Sum + Modulo program.

numbers.what: SCAN compiled model size
numbers.value: < 2,000 MLP hidden dims; up to 512 layers
numbers.quote: Because our ALTA program decomposes the task into many small steps, it can require up to 512 layers to handle the longest SCAN examples.

limitations: Limited numeric computation and no probabilistic outputs; compiled models may not reflect learned ones; encoder-only focus.
venue: Published in Transactions on Machine Learning Research (2/2025)
survey_notes: Key 'expressible is not learned' evidence for looped models: the sequential length-invariant solution exists in a weight-shared encoder but end-to-end training picks the fewest-layer shortcut. Agrees with 2607.20594 (training selects mechanism, not expressivity) though the selected mechanism differs (ALTA: shallowest; 2607.20594: serial frontier priced by budget). Trace (step-level) supervision recovers the minimal program behaviour, contrasting with 2603.21676 where per-step supervision harmed extrapolation (different supervision target: full program trace vs final-answer readout at each step).

title: Bypassing the Exponential Dependency: Looped Transformers Efficiently Learn In-context by Multi-step Gradient Descent
relevance_reason: Construction showing a linear looped transformer performs T steps of gradient descent in-context with error exp(-T/(2 kappa)), removing an exponential sample requirement.
one_sentence: Shows a linear looped transformer can explicitly run multi-step gradient descent in its hidden state for in-context linear vector generation, with error at most |alpha| exp(-T/(2 kappa)) after T loops, so O(d) well-conditioned examples suffice instead of exp(Omega(T)).
key_contributions: Lemma 4.1 / Theorem 4.2: each loop of a linear looped transformer implements one GD step on the in-context least-squares objective.

Theorem 4.5: prediction error <= |alpha| * exp(-T/(2 kappa)); with constant condition number (n = O(d)) the error decays exponentially in loops, bypassing the n = exp(Omega(T)) requirement of prior work.
Numerical check of GD convergence rates for d=4, n in {16,...,128} against the bound.

setup.model_sizes: Linear looped transformer (constructed weights Q, P)
setup.loops_test: T loops (experiments T=200 GD iterations)
setup.baselines: Prior bound of Gatmiry et al. 2024 requiring exp(Omega(T)) examples
setup.benchmarks: Synthetic linear vector generation / regression, d=4

claims.claim: Optimization/simulation: linear looped transformers implement multi-step GD in-context with error decaying exponentially in loop count when the data are well-conditioned (n = O(d)).
claims.evidence_quote: Our results demonstrate that as long as the input data has a constant condition number, e.g., n = O(d), the linear looped Transformers can achieve a small error by multi-step gradient descent during in-context learning.

claims.claim: Resource bound: after T loops the prediction error is at most |alpha| exp(-T/(2 kappa)) where kappa is the condition number of X^T X.
claims.evidence_quote: the linear looped Transformer can predict a vector output with error ≤ |α| · exp(− 2κ ) by explicitly performing multi-step gradient descent in its hidden states.

claims.claim: Prior results needed an exponential number of in-context examples in the loop count; this work removes that dependency.
claims.evidence_quote: However, their theoretical results require an exponential number of in-context examples, n = exp(Ω(T )), where T is the number of loops or passes, to achieve a reasonably low error.

numbers.what: Average condition numbers for n=16,32,64,128 at d=4
numbers.quote: The average κ values for the different sample sizes are {4.57, 3.13, 2.07, 1.62}, corresponding to n = {16, 32, 64, 128} respectively.

limitations: Linear attention, constructed (not trained) weights; 'experiments' run plain gradient descent rather than a trained transformer, so they validate the GD bound, not learnability.
survey_notes: Expressivity-side complement to the learnability result of 2410.08292 (theory_a): once loops implement GD, accuracy is bought by loops at rate exp(-T/2kappa); 2410.21698 shows the kappa dependence is necessary in depth (log kappa lower bound with stronger algorithms, sqrt kappa restricted). Note the experiments do not train any transformer.

title: Transformers discover an elementary calculation system exploiting local attention and grid-like problem representation
relevance_reason: Universal (weight-shared, recurrent) transformer with local attention on a grid and learned halting for multi-digit addition extrapolation; small task-specific model.
one_sentence: A Universal Transformer with local (convolution-like) attention over a learned grid layout of the input and PonderNet-style halting learns multi-digit, multi-operand addition and extrapolates from 10-digit training operands to hundreds or thousands of digits, though extrapolation in number of operands is weaker.
key_contributions: Architecture: Seq2Grid preprocessing into a 2D grid, local attention heads, recurrent (weight-shared) Universal Transformer core and a halting transformer with an Explore-Reinforce regularizer.
Extrapolation: trained on up to 4 operands of up to 10 digits, reaches 0.99 sequence accuracy on 2-term 602-digit additions (noGroups variant) and 0.93 on 5-6 terms.
Ablations: a fixed 12-step variant degrades operand-count extrapolation; learned halting stabilizes in steps even when more terms need more computation; failures on long carries.

setup.train_tokens_or_data: Multi-digit addition problems with up to 4 operands, each up to 10 digits

GHR: global recurrent step with nested low/high-level recurrences, input features injected each iteration; augments any message-passing backbone.

relevance_reason: Exact expressivity of recurrent (weight-shared, self-terminating) GNNs under float vs real arithmetic; graph analog of looped-model precision results.
one_sentence: Gives exact logical characterizations of recurrent GNNs that iterate a shared layer until designated termination features fire: with floats they equal the graded modal substitution calculus (GMSC), with reals an infinitary graded modal logic, and both coincide on MSO-definable properties.
key_contributions: Recurrent GNNs with floats = GMSC = R-simple aggregate-combine float GNNs (Theorem 3.2), an absolute characterization under natural float assumptions.
Recurrent GNNs with reals = omega-GML (infinitary graded modal logic).
Relative to MSO-definable properties, float and real recurrent GNNs are equally expressive; in general floats are weaker; links to distributed automata.

title: When and How Unlabeled Data Provably Improve In-Context Learning
relevance_reason: Theory shows multi-layer or looped linear attention implements EM-like polynomial estimators for semi-supervised ICL; the application loops a tabular foundation model at the prompt level, not in depth.
one_sentence: For semi-supervised in-context classification of binary GMMs, proves one-layer linear attention cannot use unlabeled demonstrations while L-layer or looped linear attention implements polynomial (EM-like) estimators sum_i a_i (X^T X)^i X^T y with degree up to O(3^L); looping TabPFN-v2 over pseudo-labels improves few-shot tabular accuracy.
key_contributions: Landscape result: the global minimum of one-layer linear attention under SS-ICL is the plug-in estimator X^T y, so it ignores unlabeled data (Theorem 1).

Depth/looping: L-layer linear attention expresses label-propagation products prod(I + c_l X^T X) or feature-propagation (X^T X)^{3^{L-1}-1}; a single layer looped L times reproduces label propagation (Proposition 2); L>=2 approaches Bayes error as n grows (Theorems 3-4).
LoopTabFM: iteratively pseudo-labeling and re-prompting TabPFN-v2 improves accuracy on most OpenML binary datasets with 10 labeled + 10 unlabeled examples; most gains in the first two iterations.

title: When Does Recurrence Become an Algorithm? Convergence Selection in Weight-Tied Looped Transformers
relevance_reason: Controlled population study of what algorithm SGD selects in weight-tied looped transformers, with tied vs untied controls at fixed effective depth and parameter count.
one_sentence: Weight-tied looped transformers trained on group word problems learn a serial 'linear computation frontier' whose speed equals training demand n/T (budget law); weight tying, not expressivity, selects it over parallel scans, and S5's learning wall is operator size, not NC1-hardness.
key_contributions: Budget law: frontier speed v tracks n_tr/T_tr with exponent 0.98+-0.04 (R^2=0.99, 23 models); extra test-time loops rescue late positions at fixed length; implies a halting rule T*=ceil(n/v).

Selection not expressivity: at fixed effective depth 12 with matched parameters, untying hurts extrapolation (S4) and blocks learning (A5, G>=3 groups); A5 (NC1-complete) is learned while S5 deadlocks until an operator-first curriculum.

Tail-saturation proposition: skip/similarity metrics are blind at fixed points; head instrument tau(n,i) (convergence-time scaling) predicts seed-level OOD generalization; replicates on easy-to-hard prefix sums with 4x extrapolation.

title: Neural Weight Norm = Kolmogorov Complexity
relevance_reason: Theory result stated for looped (iterated-until-halt) fixed-precision networks; concerns weight-decay priors rather than looped LM design.
one_sentence: Proves that for fixed-precision looped networks iterated until a halt channel fires, the minimum number of non-zero parameters (hence any Lp weight norm) needed to output a string equals its Kolmogorov complexity up to a log factor, so weight decay approximates Solomonoff's prior.
key_contributions: Sandwich bound N(s) <= K(s)+c_U and K(s) <= c_d N(s) log N(s) for fixed-precision looped networks (Theorem 4), tight at both ends (permutation witness).
Lp collapse: in fixed precision every Lp^p norm equals the non-zero parameter count up to constants, so the result is norm-agnostic.
Corollary: L2 weight decay induces an output prior matching Solomonoff's universal prior up to a polynomial factor; fixed precision is essential (real weights are super-Turing).
