title: Emergent Models: Intelligence from Tiny Substrates
relevance_reason: Cellular-automaton substrates iterating a fixed local rule for an adaptive number of steps, trained by evolutionary search; iteration-for-extrapolation lineage, not neural looped models.
one_sentence: Proposes Emergent Models, fixed-rule dynamical substrates (e.g. cellular automata) iterated for an adaptive number of steps and trained by evolutionary search, proves some are latent-universal (any partial computable function via the initial state), and shows tiny instances extrapolate exactly on simple arithmetic.
key_contributions: Latent universality (Theorem 1): with fixed update rule and interface, varying only the finite-support initial program state realizes any partial computable function.
Zoo of minimal EMs (tens to hundreds of parameters) learned by genetic algorithms; perfect extrapolation on all one-input arithmetic tasks tested (train [0,30], test [30,1000]).
Conjecture that adaptive iteration, not a single forward pass, enables extrapolation, governed by the ratio of parameters to temporal depth.

setup.model_sizes: 20-300 parameters
setup.train_tokens_or_data: Integer arithmetic on [0,30]; CartPole; MetaLife control
setup.loops_test: Adaptive
setup.benchmarks: Integer functions (e.g. x mod 4, multiplication), CartPole, MetaLife

claims.claim: Universality: some Emergent Models are latent-universal, realizing any partial computable function with the rule and interface fixed and only the initial latent state varied.
claims.evidence_quote: Theoretically, we prove that some EMs are latent-universal: with the update rule and interface held fixed, they can realize any partial computable function by varying only the initial condition of the latent state.

claims.claim: Tiny iterated substrates extrapolate exactly on simple one-input arithmetic functions in all runs.
claims.evidence_quote: Perfect extrapolation is observed, in all runs, for all oneinput tasks considered.

numbers.what: Arithmetic train vs extrapolation ranges
numbers.quote: Training is performed on inputs in [0, 30], while extrapolation is evaluated on [30, 1000].

limitations: Evolutionary search, not gradient training; simple tasks; two-input multiplication and harder tasks largely fail; robustness limitations in control.
survey_notes: Peripheral to looped LMs; shares the thesis that iterating a small fixed rule with adaptive halting drives extrapolation (cf. 2602.01651, 2606.20325). Exclude from quantitative comparisons.

title: Simulation of Graph Algorithms with Looped Transformers
relevance_reason: Constructive simulation of classic graph algorithms by constant-width looped transformers with adjacency-aware attention heads.
one_sentence: Proves by construction that a looped transformer with extra adjacency-multiplied attention heads and O(1) width simulates Dijkstra, BFS, DFS and Kosaraju's SCC (and a multitask model) for graphs of any size up to finite-precision limits, is Turing complete with constant width, and that the constructed parameters are hard to recover by training.
key_contributions: Constant-width looped transformers simulate Dijkstra (17 layers, 3 heads), BFS (17 layers), DFS (15 layers), Kosaraju SCC (22 layers, 4 heads); a 19-layer multitask model runs BFS, DFS and Dijkstra.
Parameter count independent of graph size; graph size bounded by O(1/delta_hat) and O(Omega) from finite precision.
Turing completeness with O(1) width via Graph-SUBLEQ (11 layers, 3 heads); ill-conditioning analysis shows constructed solutions are hard to reach by gradient training.

setup.model_sizes: 15-22 layers per loop body, 3-4 heads, O(1) width
setup.loops_test: Loop until algorithm termination criterion
setup.benchmarks: CLRS-style algorithms (Dijkstra, BFS, DFS, SCC); training-recovery experiments in Appendix B.4

claims.claim: Simulation: a looped transformer of constant width with adjacency-aware heads simulates Dijkstra's algorithm on rational-weighted graphs up to O(1/delta_hat) nodes.
claims.evidence_quote: There exists a looped-transformer hT in the form of (2), with 17 layers, 3 attention heads, and layer width O(1) that simulates Dijkstra's shortest path algorithm for weighted graphs with rational edge-weights

claims.claim: Parameter count does not grow with graph size, but finite precision limits the simulable graph size.
claims.evidence_quote: The number of parameters in the networks does not increase with the input graph size, which implies that the networks can simulate the above algorithms for any graph. Despite this property, we show a limit to simulation in our solution due to finite precision.

claims.claim: Universality: the architecture is Turing complete with O(1) width via an 11-layer, 3-head SUBLEQ simulation.
claims.evidence_quote: with 11 layers, 3 attention heads, and layer width O(1) that simulates SUBLEQ.

claims.claim: Learnability caveat: constructed parameters require approximating discontinuous functions, causing ill-conditioning that makes gradient-based recovery hard, worsening as tolerances shrink.
claims.evidence_quote: Despite demonstrating the existence of parameters capable of simulation, discovering them through gradient-based training is challenging.

numbers.what: Kosaraju SCC simulator size
numbers.quote: Theorem 6.4. There exists a looped-transformer hT in the form of (2), with 22 layers, 4 attention heads, and layer width O(1) that simulates Kosaraju's Strongly Connected Components algorithm

limitations: Constructive only; requires a non-standard attention head multiplied by the adjacency matrix; finite precision bounds graph size; training to recover the construction is ill-conditioned.
survey_notes: Anchor for 'looped transformers as algorithm executors' (graph section); extended to hypergraphs by 2501.10688. Explicitly flags the expressivity/learnability gap via ill-conditioning, consistent with 2410.18077 and 2607.20594.

title: Transformers Can Do Arithmetic with the Right Embeddings
relevance_reason: Main contribution is a digit positional embedding; looped transformers with input injection are a secondary, controlled ablation for length generalization.
one_sentence: Abacus positional embeddings (per-digit significance) let small transformers trained on 20-digit addition reach up to 99% on 100-digit addition; looped transformers with input injection and progressive loss further cut OOD error at fixed effective depth.
key_contributions: Abacus Embeddings: learned per-digit significance embeddings with random offset, giving 6x length extrapolation on addition (trained <=20 digits, tested to 120).

Controlled recurrence ablation at fixed effective depth 16 (16x1 to 1x16): 8x2 looped model best on OOD addition; looped model with input injection + progressive loss beats standard models with ~10x fewer parameters.
Extends to multiplication (15 digits, looped 4x4) and sorting, where looped models are best only at min-element extrapolation, not full sorting.

setup.model_sizes: 12M (1 layer x 16 recurrences) to 122M (16x1) parameters with Abacus + input injection (Table 3)
setup.train_tokens_or_data: 20 million samples per training set; cramming budget of 8 exaFLOP (one RTXA4000, 24 h); 64 exaFLOP for multiplication
setup.loops_train: Effective depth 16 split as 16x1, 8x2, 4x4, 2x8, 1x16; progressive loss mixes nominal and random fewer recurrences
setup.loops_test: Nominal recurrences (e.g. 16 for 1x16)
setup.baselines: Standard transformer (ST), ST with input injection, FIRE / NoPE / RoPE embeddings, index hints
setup.benchmarks: Multi-digit addition (ID <=20, OOD <=100, 100+ OOD to 160 digits), subtraction, multiplication up to 15 digits, array sorting

claims.claim: Abacus Embeddings with looped transformers and input injection raise OOD addition accuracy from 92.9% to 99.1% (87% error reduction) relative to the embeddings with standard architectures.
claims.regime: iso_effective_depth (effective depth 16), same data and 8 exaFLOP budget; looped model has fewer parameters
claims.evidence_quote: We show that when we combine Abacus Embeddings with input injection and looped transformers performance further improves, increasing from 92.9% to 99.1% in out of distribution accuracy, an 87% reduction in error

claims.claim: At fixed effective depth 16, an 8-layer block looped twice (8x2) halves the OOD error of the non-recurrent 16x1 model with input injection.
claims.evidence_quote: We see that a recurrent model with eight layers in the recurrent block and two recurrences is the most accurate of all effective depth 16 models, halving the error rate of a standard model with input injection in the OOD evaluation.

claims.claim: With FIRE or NoPE on 40-digit training data, the looped transformer (input injection + progressive loss) has the best OOD addition despite ~10x fewer parameters.
claims.evidence_quote: Despite having approximately 10× fewer parameters than the other models, we see that the looped transformer (recurrent, with input injection and progressive loss), achieves the best out of distribution performance using either position embedding.

claims.claim: Looping does not uniformly help: on sorting, the standard transformer has the best exact-match accuracy, while the looped transformer is best only at identifying the minimum element.
claims.evidence_quote: For sorting, different architectures appear to be better suited to different types of extrapolation, for example the looped transformer is best at extrapolating for finding the minimum element but not for sorting the whole array.

claims.claim: Length generalization reaches 6x the training length (20 to 120 digits), versus 2.5x for prior state of the art.
claims.evidence_quote: models trained with at most 20 digit operands can generalize to problems with 120 digit operands. This represents a state-of-the-art generalization factor of 6×, with the previous state of the art being only 2.5×.

numbers.what: Max OOD addition accuracy at 100 digits, trained on 20 digits, 1 GPU-day
numbers.quote: We find that training on only 20 digit numbers with a single GPU for one day, we can reach state-of-the-art performance, achieving up to 99% accuracy on 100 digit addition problems.

numbers.what: OOD addition accuracy: standard architecture with Abacus vs looped + input injection
numbers.quote: increasing from 92.9% to 99.1% in out of distribution accuracy, an 87% reduction in error compared to using the embeddings with standard architectures alone.

numbers.what: Training budget per addition run
numbers.quote: limit each training run to 8 exaFLOP of compute (a single Nvidia RTXA4000 GPU for 24 hours); for multiplication results we allow 64 exaFLOP (eight Nvidia RTXA4000 GPUs for 24 hours).

numbers.what: Input injection error reduction over Abacus baseline
numbers.quote: We find that incorporating input injection—skip connections inserted between the input layer and each decoder layer—can reduce generalization errors by 50% over the Abacus Embedding baseline.

numbers.what: Training set size
numbers.quote: For this study all training sets have 20 million samples and i = j, hence we can use one number to define the dataset

numbers.what: Total compute for main-paper results
numbers.quote: An estimate of the total compute required for all of the results presented in the main paper is 10, 039 GPU hours.

numbers.what: Parameters by configuration at effective depth 16 (16x1, 8x2, 4x4, 2x8, 1x16)

limitations: No natural-language tasks; compute-constrained from-scratch training; Abacus is absolute-style, so generalization is bounded by the offset range k; looped models not uniformly best (sorting).
venue: 38th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2024).
builds_on: Looped Transformers are Better at Learning Learning Algorithms (2311.12424)
survey_notes: One of the cleanest iso-effective-depth ablations: same effective depth 16, same 8 exaFLOP budget, varying block size vs recurrence. Optimum is a mild recurrence (8x2), not maximal (1x16), matching the 'partial sharing' finding elsewhere. Looped models are not uniformly best (sorting). Note iso-effective-depth here is not iso-param: 16x1 has 122M vs 12M for 1x16. Uses Bansal et al. progressive loss (randomized loops in training) and input injection; gradient scaling by recurrences for multiplication.
